# Model-to-Model Knowledge Transmission (M2KT): A Data-Free Framework for Cross-Model Understanding Transfer

Pratham Sorte Affiliation:  Department of Computer Science and
Engineering  
MIT-World Peace University, Pune, India  
Email: prathamsorte@mitwpu.edu.in

###### Abstract

Modern artificial intelligence systems depend heavily on large datasets
for both training and transferring knowledge between models. Knowledge
distillation, transfer learning, and dataset distillation have made such
transfers more efficient, yet they remain fundamentally data-driven: a
teacher must produce examples, logits, or gradients for a student to
learn. In this work, we introduce _Model-to-Model Knowledge Transmission
(M2KT)_, a novel paradigm for data-free conceptual transfer between
neural networks. M2KT enables models to exchange _knowledge packets_
that encapsulate structured concept embeddings, abstraction graphs,
reasoning traces, and provenance metadata. Unlike classical
distillation, M2KT operates primarily in concept space rather than
example space, and it does not require labeled datasets or
teacher-generated logits during transfer. We formalize the notion of
concept manifolds, introduce an inter-model alignment mapping between
teacher and student latent spaces, and derive a composite loss that
enforces geometric, structural, and reasoning consistency, together with
explicit safety constraints. We further present detailed algorithmic
procedures for teacher-side packet generation and student-side ingestion
and verification. Experiments on symbolic reasoning with large language
models show that M2KT can achieve 85–90% of teacher performance while
reducing data usage by over 98% compared to standard knowledge
distillation. This work establishes a theoretical and practical
foundation for data-free AI-to-AI education and self-improving model
ecosystems.

###### Index Terms: 

Model-to-Model Learning, Knowledge Distillation, Meta-Learning,
Data-Free AI, Concept Embeddings, Neural Representation Alignment,
Federated Learning, Machine Teaching, AI-to-AI Communication, Model
Merging.

## I Introduction

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance across vision,
language, and multi-modal tasks. These advances are driven primarily by
two factors: (i) massive datasets and (ii) large-scale compute. Even
mechanisms for transferring knowledge between models—such as knowledge
distillation and transfer learning—remain strongly tied to data: the
teacher must generate abundant outputs (e.g., logits, soft labels, or
feature activations) to supervise a student.

This data-centric paradigm leads to several limitations:

- •
  Privacy and security: Raw training data may be sensitive and cannot
  always be shared or regenerated.
- •
  Compute and latency: Generating large volumes of teacher outputs is
  computationally expensive.
- •
  Architectural rigidity: Many methods assume similar architectures or
  dimensions (e.g., for weight sharing or model merging).
- •
  Limited abstraction transfer: Distillation largely matches outputs,
  not the underlying conceptual understanding or reasoning processes.

Humans, by contrast, rarely learn purely from raw datasets. Teachers
convey abstractions, high-level concepts, and structured reasoning
patterns that learners internalize and reuse. This motivates the central
question of this paper:

Can one model teach another by transmitting structured understanding
directly, without using training examples or logits?

To address this, we propose _Model-to-Model Knowledge Transmission
(M2KT)_, a framework in which a teacher model exports abstract
_knowledge packets_ consisting of concept embeddings, saliency and
attention patterns, and reasoning traces. A student model then ingests
these packets through a dedicated _Concept Alignment Layer (CAL)_, which
maps the teacher’s concept manifold into the student’s latent space. A
verification and safety module evaluates whether the transferred
knowledge behaves as expected and rejects or rolls back problematic
updates.

The contributions of this paper are:

- •
  We introduce the M2KT paradigm for data-free conceptual transfer
  between neural networks.
- •
  We formalize concept manifolds, define inter-model alignment mappings,
  and derive a composite loss that jointly enforces geometric,
  structural, reasoning, and safety constraints.
- •
  We design a modular architecture comprising a teacher, knowledge
  packet generator, optional knowledge broker, student with alignment
  layer, and verification and safety auditor.
- •
  We provide detailed algorithms for teacher-side packet generation and
  student-side ingestion and verification suitable for practical
  implementation.
- •
  We present preliminary experimental results on symbolic reasoning
  tasks that demonstrate promising transfer efficiency with drastically
  reduced data requirements.

## II Background and Related Work

This section situates M2KT in the context of existing approaches to
model compression, transfer, and meta-learning.

### II-A Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation (KD) \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] trains a smaller
_student_ model to match the softened output distribution (logits) of a
larger _teacher_ model. KD has become a standard technique for
compressing large models and is widely used in practice.

Despite its success, KD has several important limitations:

- •
  It requires generating a large number of teacher outputs for a
  possibly extensive dataset (real or synthetic).
- •
  It primarily enforces output-level agreement, which may not capture
  deeper conceptual or causal structure learned by the teacher.
- •
  It is tightly coupled to the availability of input examples and their
  distribution.

In contrast, M2KT attempts to transfer a compact representation of
conceptual knowledge directly, without requiring examples during the
transfer phase.

### II-B Dataset Distillation

Dataset distillation techniques \[[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\]
construct small synthetic datasets that approximately preserve the
training signal of much larger datasets. These synthetic datasets can
then be used to train new models with significantly fewer examples.

However, dataset distillation still uses _examples_ (albeit synthetic),
and student training remains dataset-driven. M2KT aims instead to
operate primarily in concept space, transmitting latent abstractions
rather than example-level data.

### II-C Transfer Learning and Parameter-Efficient Adaptation

Transfer learning adapts pre-trained models to new tasks through
fine-tuning, often with parameter-efficient methods such as adapters or
low-rank updates. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] is a
prominent approach where low-rank matrices are added to frozen
pre-trained weights, enabling task-specific adaptation with a small
number of trainable parameters.

M2KT is complementary: it assumes models may have parameter-efficient
modules (e.g., LoRA, adapters) and uses these as the primary interface
for ingesting abstract knowledge packets from other models.

### II-D Federated Learning

Federated learning \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] trains models on decentralized
data by aggregating parameter updates from multiple clients without
centralizing raw data. While this preserves privacy to some degree, it
still relies on gradient updates being derived from local datasets.

M2KT can be seen as an extreme form of federated or collaborative
learning in which only concept-level information (not gradients or data)
is shared between nodes.

### II-E Meta-Learning and Machine Teaching

Meta-learning, or “learning to learn,” trains models that can adapt
rapidly to new tasks with few examples \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. Many
meta-learning algorithms explicitly focus on learning initializations or
update rules that generalize across tasks.

M2KT shares conceptual goals with meta-learning but focuses specifically
on _cross-model conceptual transfer_, rather than optimizing adaptation
across task distributions.

## III Problem Setup and High-Level Overview

### III-A Teacher and Student Models

Let the teacher model be denoted by

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       T(x)=h_{T}(f_{T}(x)),
       ```                    |     | (1) |

where $`f_{T}(\cdot)`$ is the feature encoder mapping inputs $`x`$ to
latent representations and $`h_{T}(\cdot)`$ is the task head.

Similarly, the student model is given by

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       S(x)=h_{S}(f_{S}(x)),
       ```                    |     | (2) |

with its own encoder $`f_{S}(\cdot)`$ and head $`h_{S}(\cdot)`$. The
teacher and student may differ significantly in architecture, depth, and
number of parameters.

### III-B Concept Manifolds

We interpret the teacher encoder $`f_{T}`$ as defining a _latent
manifold_ of representations:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{M}_{T}=\{f_{T}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{T}}.
``` |  | (3) |

Within this manifold, we identify a discrete set of *concept embeddings*

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{T}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{n}\}\subset\mathcal{M}_{T},
       ```                                                       |     | (4) |

where each $`c_{k}`$ corresponds to a conceptual unit (e.g., “addition
in symbolic arithmetic,” “subject-verb agreement,” “causal relation type
A”).

The student encoder defines a corresponding manifold

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{M}_{S}=\{f_{S}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{S}}.
``` |  | (5) |

### III-C Goal of M2KT

M2KT seeks to:

- •
  Extract a set of concept embeddings and associated structural
  information from $`\mathcal{M}_{T}`$.
- •
  Package these into compact *knowledge packets*.
- •
  Transmit the packets to the student model without sending training
  examples.
- •
  Align the student’s latent space $`\mathcal{M}_{S}`$ to incorporate
  these concepts via a trainable *Concept Alignment Layer*.
- •
  Verify that the student’s behavior has improved on relevant tasks and
  remains safe.

## IV M2KT Framework and Architecture

### IV-A System Components

The M2KT framework consists of the following core components:

1.  1.
    Teacher Model (T): A pretrained model possessing useful conceptual
    knowledge.
2.  2.
    Concept Extractor (CE): A procedure that extracts concept
    embeddings, attention maps, and reasoning traces from $`T`$.
3.  3.
    Knowledge Packet Generator (KPG): Builds structured knowledge
    packets from extracted information.
4.  4.
    Knowledge Broker (KB) (optional): Verifies provenance, integrity,
    and safety of packets before distribution.
5.  5.
    Student Model (S): A model to be improved via knowledge
    transmission.
6.  6.
    Concept Alignment Layer (CAL): A small trainable module in $`S`$
    that maps teacher concept embeddings into $`\mathcal{M}_{S}`$.
7.  7.
    Verifier & Safety Auditor (VS): Evaluates functional performance and
    detects harmful or anomalous behavior resulting from transmission.

### IV-B Knowledge Packet Structure

A knowledge packet $`P`$ is defined as

|     |                       |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P=\{C,A,R,M,\sigma\},
       ```                    |     | (6) |

where:

- •
  $`C=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{n}\}`$: concept embeddings from
  $`\mathcal{M}_{T}`$.
- •
  $`A`$: associated attention or saliency maps (e.g., layer-wise
  attention distributions).
- •
  $`R`$: reasoning traces or abstraction graphs describing logical or
  causal relationships between states.
- •
  $`M`$: metadata (teacher identity, timestamp, training domain,
  confidence scores).
- •
  $`\sigma`$: a digital signature for integrity and provenance
  verification.

### IV-C Concept Alignment Layer in the Student

The student model is augmented with a *Concept Alignment Layer*,
$`\phi_{\theta}`$, parameterized by $`\theta`$, which maps teacher
concept embeddings into the student latent space:

|     |                                                                |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \phi_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{T}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{S}}.
       ```                                                             |     | (7) |

The CAL may be implemented using a small MLP, adapter-like low-rank
layers, or attention-based projection.

Given teacher concept $`c_{k}`$, the projected embedding is

|     |                                   |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{c}_{k}=\phi_{\theta}(c_{k}).
       ```                                |     | (8) |

## V Theoretical Formulation

### V-A Concept Manifold and Extraction

The teacher’s encoder $`f_{T}`$ induces a concept manifold
$`\mathcal{M}_{T}`$. We assume a concept extraction operator

|     |                                                               |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{Extract}_{T}:\mathcal{M}_{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{T},
       ```                                                            |     | (9) |

which returns a discrete set of concepts

|     |                              |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{T}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{n}\}.
       ```                           |     | (10) |

Practically, $`\text{Extract}_{T}`$ may be implemented using:

- •
  Clustering of latent representations for specific prompts.
- •
  Gradient-based attribution to isolate features relevant to particular
  tasks.
- •
  Concept bottleneck models that explicitly represent concepts as
  intermediate variables.

### V-B Student Manifold and Alignment Mapping

The student encoder $`f_{S}`$ defines manifold $`\mathcal{M}_{S}`$. Our
objective is to learn an alignment mapping

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \phi_{\theta}:\mathcal{M}_{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{S},
       ```                                                       |     | (11) |

parameterized by $`\theta`$, such that
$`\hat{c}_{k}=\phi_{\theta}(c_{k})`$ is compatible with native student
representations for the same concept.

Let $`c_{k}^{S}`$ denote the student’s internal embedding associated
with concept $`k`$, obtained via probing or auxiliary training. A basic
geometric alignment loss is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{geo}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left\|\phi_{\theta}(c_{k})-c_{k}^{S}\right\|_{2}^{2}.
``` |  | (12) |

### V-C Structural and Attention Consistency

Knowledge packets may include attention or saliency maps $`A_{T}`$ from
the teacher and $`A_{S}`$ from the student. We define a structural
consistency loss:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{struct}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\|A_{T}^{(k)}-A_{S}^{(k)}\|_{1},
``` |  | (13) |

which encourages the student to focus on similar regions or tokens when
processing concept-related inputs.

### V-D Reasoning Trace Alignment

Let the teacher’s reasoning trace for a concept-specific task instance
be:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{T}=(s_{1}\rightarrow s_{2}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow s_{m}),
``` |  | (14) |

and the student’s corresponding reasoning trace be:

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{S}=(t_{1}\rightarrow t2\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow t_{m}).
       ```                                                            |     | (15) |

Each state $`s_{i}`$ and $`t_{i}`$ represents an intermediate
representation or symbolic element. We define a reasoning consistency
loss:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{reason}}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\text{CE}(s_{i},t_{i}),
``` |  | (16) |

where CE denotes a cross-entropy or distance metric over symbolic or
embedded states.

### V-E Safety Constraints and Loss

To avoid transmitting harmful, biased, or adversarial behavior, we
define a safe concept set
$`\mathcal{C}_{\text{safe}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{T}`$ and require that
all transmitted concepts satisfy:

|     |                                                  |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       c_{k}\in\mathcal{C}_{\text{safe}}\quad\forall k.
       ```                                               |     | (17) |

Violations are penalized via a safety loss:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{safety}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\text{Penalty}(c_{k}),
``` |  | (18) |

where Penalty can be derived from toxicity detectors, bias measures, or
anomaly scores on synthetic probes.

### V-F Composite Objective

The overall alignment objective is a weighted combination:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\text{geo}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\text{struct}}+\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\text{reason}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{safety}},
``` |  | (19) |

where $`\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\lambda`$ are hyperparameters controlling
the relative importance of each term. Training proceeds by updating
$`\theta`$ to minimize $`\mathcal{L}`$, typically with gradient-based
optimization while keeping most of the student’s core parameters frozen
to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

### V-G Information-Theoretic View of M2KT

From an information-theoretic standpoint, the teacher’s knowledge about
a task can be viewed as a distribution $`p_{T}(y\mid x)`$ and an
internal representation distribution over $`\mathcal{M}_{T}`$. Classical
distillation minimizes a divergence such as

|     |                                                              |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{T}(y\mid x)\,\|\,p_{S}(y\mid x)\big),
       ```                                                           |     | (20) |

using example-level inputs $`x`$.

In contrast, M2KT aims to minimize a divergence directly in concept
space:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{T}(c\mid k)\,\|\,p_{S}(\phi_{\theta}(c)\mid k)\big),
``` |  | (21) |

where $`k`$ indexes high-level concepts, $`c`$ is a concept embedding,
and $`p_{T}`$, $`p_{S}`$ describe distributions over latent
representations conditioned on the same conceptual index. Intuitively,
we are matching *conceptual sufficient statistics* rather than raw
sample-level conditionals.

Under mild assumptions (e.g., concepts forming an approximate sufficient
statistic for task performance), one can argue that minimizing this
concept-level divergence yields lower-bounded performance on downstream
tasks — even in the absence of direct example-level supervision during
the transfer phase. A full formal proof is left for future work, but
this suggests that M2KT acts as a compressed channel for transmitting
mutual information about the task from the teacher to the student.

### V-H Manifold Alignment Illustration

The manifold alignment process can be understood as points on the
teacher manifold being mapped by $`\phi_{\theta}`$ into the student
manifold, such that corresponding concept embeddings are brought into
geometric and structural agreement in the student’s latent space.

## VI Algorithmic Description

### VI-A Teacher-Side Packet Generation

0:  Teacher model $`T`$, concept specification set $`\mathcal{K}`$.

0:  Knowledge packet $`P=\{C,A,R,M,\sigma\}`$.

1:  Initialize $`C\leftarrow\emptyset`$, $`A\leftarrow\emptyset`$,
$`R\leftarrow\emptyset`$.

2:  for each concept $`k\in\mathcal{K}`$ do

3:   $`c_{k}\leftarrow\text{ExtractEmbedding}(T,k)`$

4:   $`a_{k}\leftarrow\text{ExtractAttention}(T,k)`$

5:   $`r_{k}\leftarrow\text{ExtractReasoningTrace}(T,k)`$

6:   Append $`c_{k}`$ to $`C`$

7:   Append $`a_{k}`$ to $`A`$

8:   Append $`r_{k}`$ to $`R`$

9:  end for

10:  $`M\leftarrow\text{BuildMetadata}(T,\mathcal{K})`$

11:  $`\sigma\leftarrow\text{Sign}(C,A,R,M)`$

12:  return $`P=\{C,A,R,M,\sigma\}`$

Algorithm 1 Teacher-Side Knowledge Packet Generation

### VI-B Student-Side Ingestion and Alignment

0:  Student model $`S`$ with CAL $`\phi_{\theta}`$, packet
$`P=\{C,A,R,M,\sigma\}`$.

0:  Updated student model $`S^{\prime}`$ or rollback upon failure.

1:  Verify $`\sigma`$ and integrity of $`P`$.

2:  if verification fails then

3:   Reject packet and abort.

4:  end if

5:  Initialize total loss $`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow 0`$.

6:  for each concept $`c_{k}`$ in $`C`$ do

7:   $`\hat{c}_{k}\leftarrow\phi_{\theta}(c_{k})`$

8:   $`c_{k}^{S}\leftarrow\text{ProbeStudentConcept}(S,k)`$

9:
  $`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}+\|\hat{c}_{k}-c_{k}^{S}\|_{2}^{2}`$

10:   (Optionally incorporate structural and reasoning losses.)

11:  end for

12:  $`\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}`$ {Update
CAL only}

13:  Run safety and performance probes on $`S`$ to obtain scores.

14:  if probes indicate degradation or unsafe behavior then

15:   Roll back $`\theta`$ to previous checkpoint.

16:   Log incident and mark packet as unsafe.

17:  else

18:   Accept updated student $`S^{\prime}`$.

19:  end if

Algorithm 2 Student-Side Packet Ingestion and Alignment

## VII Experimental Setup

### VII-A Models and Tasks

To evaluate M2KT, we conduct preliminary experiments on symbolic
reasoning tasks. The setup is as follows:

- •
  Teacher: A 7B-parameter large language model (LLM) fine-tuned on
  symbolic arithmetic and logical reasoning benchmarks.
- •
  Student: A 120M-parameter transformer-based model with significantly
  smaller capacity.
- •
  Task: Zero-shot and few-shot evaluation on arithmetic expressions and
  simple logical inference tasks.

### VII-B Baseline: Knowledge Distillation

As a baseline, we perform standard knowledge distillation in which the
teacher generates soft labels for a large set of prompts, and the
student is trained to match these distributions.

### VII-C M2KT Protocol

For M2KT, we:

1.  1.
    Use probing and clustering to extract approximately 1,000 concept
    embeddings for distinct reasoning patterns.
2.  2.
    Collect attention patterns for relevant layers and extract reasoning
    traces on a small curated set of teacher internal chains.
3.  3.
    Package these into knowledge packets and transmit them to the
    student.
4.  4.
    Train only the Concept Alignment Layer and a small auxiliary head
    using synthetic consistency probes generated from the concept
    embeddings, without using real training examples.

### VII-D Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate:

- •
  Downstream Accuracy: Student performance on reasoning benchmarks.
- •
  Transfer Efficiency (TE):

  |  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|----|
  |  |
  ``` math
  \text{TE}=\frac{\text{Student Accuracy}}{\text{Teacher Accuracy}}.
  ``` |  | (22) |
- •
  Data Usage: Number of teacher-generated examples/logits used during
  transfer.
- •
  Compute Cost: Approximate FLOPs consumed during distillation vs. M2KT.

## VIII Results

### VIII-A Quantitative Comparison

|                            |              |          |
|----------------------------|--------------|----------|
| Metric                     | KD           | M2KT     |
| Teacher Accuracy (%)       | 100          | 100      |
| Student Accuracy (%)       | 91           | 87       |
| Transfer Efficiency (TE)   | 0.91         | 0.87     |
| Teacher Outputs Used       | $`\sim`$150k | 0        |
| Concept Embeddings Used    | 0            | 1,000    |
| Data Movement              | High         | Very Low |
| Cross-Architecture Support | Limited      | Strong   |

TABLE I: Comparison between Knowledge Distillation (KD) and M2KT on
symbolic reasoning tasks.

M2KT achieves approximately $`87\%`$ of teacher performance with
negligible example-level data movement, suggesting that concept-level
transfer is feasible and effective.

### VIII-B Qualitative Observations

Qualitatively, the student models trained via M2KT:

- •
  Exhibit improved robustness on tasks that require multi-step
  reasoning.
- •
  Show attention patterns more similar to the teacher in
  concept-relevant regions.
- •
  Display fewer overfitting artifacts on specific prompts, consistent
  with receiving abstract guidance rather than example-specific
  corrections.

## IX Discussion

### IX-A Advantages of M2KT

M2KT offers several advantages over traditional data-based transfer:

- •
  Data-free transmission: No need for large datasets or
  teacher-generated logits during transfer.
- •
  Privacy preservation: Sensitive training data need not be exposed or
  regenerated.
- •
  Architectural flexibility: Concept embeddings and alignment mappings
  can operate across heterogeneous architectures.
- •
  Modularity: Knowledge packets can be combined, versioned, and
  composed, enabling reusability of learned skills.

### IX-B Limitations

However, M2KT also faces important challenges:

- •
  Concept extraction difficulty: Robustly identifying meaningful
  concepts in latent space is non-trivial.
- •
  Alignment complexity: Learning $`\phi_{\theta}`$ that generalizes well
  requires careful design and sufficient probes.
- •
  Safety risks: Subliminal transfer of undesirable behaviors or hidden
  circuits is a genuine concern, requiring strong verification and
  provenance mechanisms.

## X Future Work

Future directions for M2KT include:

- •
  Multi-teacher aggregation: Combining packets from multiple teachers
  and resolving conflicts or redundancies.
- •
  Emergent teaching protocols: Allowing models to develop compressed
  communication codes for knowledge transmission.
- •
  Standardized packet formats: Developing interoperable specifications
  for knowledge packets, including signatures and safety annotations.
- •
  Theoretical guarantees: Providing bounds on transfer efficiency,
  safety, and robustness under concept-level updates.

## XI Conclusion

We introduced Model-to-Model Knowledge Transmission (M2KT), a new
framework for transferring conceptual knowledge between neural networks
without moving example-level data. By operating in concept space and
employing a dedicated alignment layer, M2KT enables data-free AI-to-AI
education while preserving privacy and supporting heterogeneous
architectures. Our theoretical framework, detailed algorithms, and
preliminary experiments suggest that M2KT is a promising direction for
building self-improving, collaborative AI ecosystems.
